 Workers get a raise, but everyone had to give something up
 An agreement on next year's wage increases was reached at a tripartite negotiating session between the government, employers, and employees — the Permanent Consultation Forum of the Competitive Sector and the Government (VKF) — on Thursday. 
 Corporate 
 20. November 2026 6:27 
 Under the agreement, the gross minimum wage will rise by 7.5 percent to 347,000 forints, while the guaranteed minimum wage will increase by 6.1 percent to 396,000 forints, András Kármán, the finance minister, announced on his Facebook page.
 Including the planned tax credit, employees not entitled to other personal income tax relief could see the net minimum wage rise by 17.2 percent — nearly 37,000 forints per month — while the guaranteed minimum wage could increase by 13.3 percent, or around 33,000 forints per month, he added.
 The ministers stressed that during the 2027 wage negotiations, the government sought to strike a balance between meaningfully increasing employee incomes and preserving the capacity of businesses to bear costs.
 Through the process of bridging the initially divergent positions of employers and employees, a tripartite agreement was reached that simultaneously serves to increase workers’ purchasing power, maintain employment stability, and ensure broad social legitimacy for the regulation.
 Once this year’s agreement has been concluded, the parties will work together on a medium-term, formula-based arrangement that can guarantee the fair determination of nominal wages in line with economic performance, according to the ministers’ post.
 Ákos Kalmár, a board member of the National Association of Employers and Industrialists (MGYOSZ), told MTI following the meeting that employers and employees had reached a bilateral agreement recommending a general 5 percent wage increase for companies operating in the competitive sector next year, taking into account the economic capacity of certain industries.
 According to the MGYOSZ board member, both employers and employees are moderately satisfied with next year’s wage agreement. He noted that the negotiating parties had started very far apart with their original proposals, and everyone had to make concessions in the interest of reaching an agreement.
 According to a statement sent by MGYOSZ to MTI, the organisation considers the agreement an important compromise, while stressing that improving the economic conditions for businesses is also necessary for wage increases to be sustainable. “The agreement required compromise from all parties.
 The level of the wage increase can be agreed upon, but the question of how to fund it cannot be decided at the negotiating table. Businesses must generate that on the market,” Ákos Kalmár said in the statement.
 According to the organisation’s statement, when determining the minimum wage, the income situation of the lowest earners had to be weighed alongside economic performance capacity, while in the case of the guaranteed wage minimum, greater weight was given to considerations arising from businesses’ financial capacity and labour market conditions.
 Róbert Zlati, president of the Hungarian Trade Union Confederation (MASZSZ), told MTI that a good agreement had been reached under the present circumstances, and that the search for compromise had helped in reaching the deal.
 He added that the letter of intent signed at the meeting also includes a commitment to developing a medium-term wage catch-up strategy.
 Jácint Hatvani, president of LIGA Trade Unions, commented on the results achieved at the VKF meeting in a statement sent to MTI, saying that while the expectation had not been met regarding the gross minimum wage, it had been met in terms of the net minimum wage — namely, that Hungary fulfil the ratified minimum wage directive.
 The goal naturally remains, and they would like the gross figure to also reflect the minimum wage reaching 50 percent of the regular average earnings, but they understand the concerns of the economy and employers, and have made concessions from the values set by the three-year agreement.
 Jácint Hatvani highlighted that the rate of increase in the guaranteed wage minimum had also been successfully raised above the level proposed by employers.
 The large gap between the wage increase applicable to workers in positions requiring at least a secondary education or vocational qualification and the minimum wage would, over the long term, cause the two types of wage floors to converge, which is why the employee side wanted the proportional difference between the minimum wage and the guaranteed minimum wage to be maintained in 2027 as well.
 A compromise agreement was reached on this point, which the employee side considers acceptable, he added.
